research_topic: SDK and Plugin Architecture - Extension Host Isolation, Capability Security, and Supply Chain Risk
transcript_summary: ADR 0018 defines the architecture spine for the Tribunus SDK and Plugin system. The existing ADR covers: SDK thesis (runtime-contract client), architecture layers (@tribunus/protocol, @tribunus/client, @tribunus/plugin), plugin system design (declarative manifests, contribution categories vs capability classes, capability model, governance pipeline, extension-host isolation, receipts, revocation), trust kernel security model (4 layers: technical confinement, capability governance, provenance/accountability, Dharma overlay), trust lanes, extension store as trust ledger, MCP integration strategy, VS Code/Chrome patterns to adopt/avoid, and non-goals. Deep research was conducted on: VS Code Extension API (Extension Host isolation, activation events, contribution points, AI integration 2026), Chrome Manifest V3 (fully deprecated V2 by 2026, no remote code, service workers, DNR, granular permissions), extension isolation patterns (process isolation, IPC, capability-scoped handles), plugin manifest formats, plugin security models (least privilege, capability-based, permission escalation detection), extension stores/trust (VS Code Marketplace, Chrome Web Store, npm security crisis 2026), auto-update security (silent update risks, permission escalation, manifest diff), plugin signing/verification (code signing, checksums, reproducible builds), dependency risk (supply chain attacks, lockfile verification, pnpm v11 mitigations), and UCAN for plugin capability grants.

research_findings.title: VS Code Extension API Architecture
research_findings.finding: Extensions run in a separate Extension Host process, isolated from the main UI process. Three host types: Local Node.js, Web, and Remote. Lazy activation via declarative activationEvents (onLanguage, onCommand, onView, onStartupFinished). Contribution points in package.json enables declarative registration of commands, menus, views, languages, themes, etc. without running extension code. 2026 emphasis: AI integration (chatInstructions, chatPromptFiles), web support, continued granular permissions discussions.

research_findings.title: Chrome Extension Manifest V3
research_findings.finding: MV3 is a comprehensive security overhaul. By 2026, Manifest V2 is fully deprecated. Key changes: no remotely hosted code, Declarative Net Request API replaces blocking webRequest, service workers replace persistent background pages, stricter CSP, granular permission model with separate host_permissions. Service workers are ephemeral (30s inactivity timeout), event-driven, no DOM access, must use storage APIs.

research_findings.title: Extension Isolation Patterns
research_findings.finding: Three core patterns: (1) Process isolation - OS-enforced separate memory spaces per extension/plugin, preventing cross-contamination. (2) Message passing (IPC) - safe communication via send/receive through kernel mediation, avoiding shared memory. (3) Capability-scoped handles - unforgeable tokens encapsulating object ID + access rights, enabling least-privilege delegation. Browsers use process isolation per tab/extension; VS Code uses Extension Host process separation. Capabilities are (object_id, access_rights) tuples supporting delegation and attenuation.

research_findings.title: Plugin Manifest Formats
research_findings.finding: Two dominant formats: Chrome manifest.json (MV3) and VS Code package.json. Both are JSON-based declarative metadata. Chrome focuses on web permissions, host access, content scripts, service workers, CSP. VS Code extends Node.js package.json with activationEvents, contributes section, extensionDependencies, engine compatibility. Common principles: unique identifiers, versioning, declarative permissions/hooks, marketplace metadata.

research_findings.title: Plugin Security Models
research_findings.finding: Three pillars: (1) Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) - grant minimum access needed; increasingly automated with continuous monitoring; aligned with Zero Trust. (2) Capability-based security - unforgeable tokens shift from 'who you are' to 'what you can do'; enables granular control, dynamic revocation, secure delegation. (3) Permission escalation detection - AI-powered behavioral analysis for sleeper agents, automated vulnerability scanning, log analysis, CVE monitoring. Real attacks (CVE-2026-6226, CVE-2026-6741) demonstrate the threat landscape.

research_findings.title: Extension Stores and Trust
research_findings.finding: VS Code Marketplace uses malware scanning (Microsoft Defender), dynamic sandbox testing, signature verification on install, secret scanning, impersonation prevention, block list, community reporting. Chrome Web Store uses ML + human review pipeline, 2SV required, privacy policy mandatory, code quality enforced, Safety Check alerts. npm supply chain in 2026 is under severe attack - malicious packages up 73% in 2025; 10,000+ malicious packages detected. Major incidents: Shai-Hulud worm (796 packages), Axios hijack (100M+ weekly downloads, March 2026), Red Hat Cloud Services compromise, IronWorm (Rust-built self-replicating malware). pnpm v11 mitigations: strictDepBuilds, minimumReleaseAge, trustPolicy.

research_findings.title: Auto-Update Security Risks
research_findings.finding: Auto-updates essential for patching vulnerabilities but create attack vectors. Silent updates amplify risks: attackers compromise developer accounts or exploit update systems to push malicious versions, creating 'sleeper agent' extensions that start benign and turn malicious. Permission escalation on update is critical: extensions can silently gain <all_urls> access without user reauthorization, especially for third-party-installed extensions. Manifest diff detection (monitoring permission changes between versions) is crucial. CVE-2026-0628, CVE-2026-11092 document policy enforcement bypasses. Manifest V3's explicit host_permissions and no remote code help but effectiveness still being evaluated.

research_findings.title: Plugin Signature and Verification
research_findings.finding: Code signing: developer digitally signs code using CA-issued certificate; OS/app verifies signature on install (hash comparison). Chrome CRX files embed public key + signature; invalid signature aborts installation. VS Code Marketplace signs all extensions; verified on install. Grafana categorizes plugin signatures (Core/Signed/Invalid/Modified/Unsigned) and refuses to load unsigned. Reproducible builds allow independent verification that binary matches source code. SHA-256/SHA-512 preferred for tamper detection.

research_findings.title: Dependency Risk Analysis
research_findings.finding: Supply chain security for plugins in 2026 under active attack. npm ecosystem: 73% increase in malicious packages in 2025, 10K+ detections, double 2024. Attackers exploit trusted distribution channels, OIDC token manipulation, dependency confusion, compromised maintainer accounts. Key incidents: Axios hijack (March 2026, North Korean actor, 100M+ weekly downloads, provenance bypass), Red Hat Cloud Services (June 2026, compromised employee GitHub, 30+ packages), IronWorm (June 2026, Rust-built self-replicating malware, 36 npm packages), Shai-Hulud worm (2025, registry-native worm, 796 packages, 132M monthly downloads). Mitigations: pnpm v11 strictDepBuilds, minimumReleaseAge, trustPolicy; npm audit signatures; version pinning, lockfiles, private registry proxies.

research_findings.title: UCAN for Plugin Capability Grants
research_findings.finding: UCAN (User Controlled Authorization Networks) is a decentralized, user-originated authorization scheme using public-key cryptography. Extends JWT with capability/resource model. Users create cryptographic key pairs; capabilities are unforgeable tokens encoding (action, resource) pairs. Key feature: delegation chains - users issue UCANs to delegate authority without sharing private keys, creating verifiable proof chains. Scoped authority enables fine-grained constraints (time limits, resource subsets, custom restrictions). Attenuation ensures delegated capabilities never exceed parent permissions. Open-source specification, community-driven. Applied to decentralized storage, API access, IoT, Web3. Ideal model for plugin permission systems: each plugin gets attenuated UCAN for its scope.

implementation_specs.title: Extension Host Process Isolation
implementation_specs.description: Define the concrete process model for the Tribunus extension host. Plugins MUST run in an isolated process, not the Electron main process. Must define the IPC protocol, startup lifecycle, failure recovery, and resource limits. Implement capability-scoped handles for all plugin-runtime communication.
acceptance_criteria: Plugins execute in a separate OS process from the Electron main process
Plugin crashes do not affect the main runtime process
All plugin-runtime communication goes through a typed message boundary
Capability handles are unforgeable and scoped to (resource, action) tuples
Extension host lifecycle: start, activate, execute, deactivate, terminate
Extension host can be restarted independently of the runtime

implementation_patterns.name: Extension Host via child_process.fork
implementation_patterns.description: Spawn extension host as a forked Node.js process with dedicated IPC channel. Each plugin gets its own isolated context within the host. VS Code uses this pattern.

implementation_patterns.name: Capability Handle Pattern
implementation_patterns.description: Capability handles are unforgeable tokens wrapping (resource, rights, constraints) triples. Runtime creates handles; plugins receive them through IPC. Attenuation creates restricted child handles.

implementation_patterns.name: IPC Message Boundary Pattern
implementation_patterns.description: Define a typed message protocol for all plugin-runtime communication. Each message has a type, payload, capability handle reference, and receipt correlation ID. Runtime validates capability before dispatching.
